b: The probe follows claims of dumping margins of up to 143% and covers solid-sawn timber and laminated veneer lumber, with local producers warning of mounting pressure on the domestic timber industry.
Australia’s trade investigation will examine allegations of dumping and subsidies involving structural timber imports from China (Image: Unsplash)

The Australian Trade Remedies Commission has launched an anti-dumping and countervailing investigation into structural timber imports from China, following allegations that the products are being sold at unfairly low prices and subsidised, putting pressure on domestic manufacturers.

Announced on 16 Nov 2026, the investigation will examine claims that Chinese imports are undercutting Australian producers, threatening local jobs, investment and regional communities dependent on the timber industry. Australian producers have alleged dumping margins of up to 143%.
“Australian timber workers and producers deserve a level playing field,” said Michael O’Connor, national secretary of the Timber, Furnishing and Textiles Union (TFTU).

“Fair competition matters for local jobs, the families who depend on them and the regional communities built around our timber industry,” he said. “That means backing Australian manufacturing jobs and ensuring local producers aren’t undermined by dumped imports.”
The potential impact on regional employment follows previous job losses in the sector. In Nov 2025, 73 workers lost their jobs when the AKD sawmill in Yarram, Gippsland, closed.

The investigation covers structural timber used in residential, commercial and industrial construction, whether solid-sawn or engineered, such as laminated veneer lumber (LVL), and whether treated or untreated, with a cross-sectional area of less than 150 sq cm.
Plywood, glue-laminated timber (glulam), cross-laminated timber (CLT) and prefabricated I-joists are excluded.
The applicants are the Australian Forest Products Association, Associated Kiln Driers, Hyne & Son, OneFortyOne Wood Products and Timberlink Australia.

The investigation period runs from 1 Jul 2025 to 30 Jun 2026. A preliminary affirmative determination could be made as early as 15 Jan 2027, with the commission’s final recommendation due by 20 Apr 2027.
O’Connor said protecting domestic timber manufacturing from unfair trade was important to Australia’s long-term economic security and manufacturing capacity.

“Our union has long been at the forefront of the fight for stronger anti-dumping laws,” he said. “Strong anti-dumping laws aren’t just about defending jobs today — they’re about ensuring Australia retains the sovereign manufacturing capability we need for the future.”

He added that a resilient housing sector depended on a strong domestic supply chain for timber and other building materials. Weakening local production, he warned, could leave the country more reliant on imports and expose it to higher construction costs.

“If we allow unfair trade to hollow out local industry, we risk becoming dependent on imports and paying the price through higher building costs down the track,” he said. “A strong Australian timber industry is good for workers, good for housing and good for the country.”
